landscape: Research on political parties rests on two families of position data. Content analyses of party programmes are led by the Manifesto Project, whose coding of election manifestos reaches back to 1920 and now spans 67 countries. Expert surveys are led by the Chapel Hill Expert Survey in Europe and by V-Party, the Global Party Survey and POPPA worldwide. Older surveys (Laver-Hunt, Huber-Inglehart, Ray, Benoit-Laver) are frozen but still used for long-run comparison. Party Facts links party identifiers across more than 60 external datasets, which makes it the practical starting point for merging any of them.

Data on party organisation and linkage have grown in the last decade. The Political Party Database codes statutes and resources, DALP measures clientelistic and programmatic linkage, and several new datasets cover intra-party democracy, party personnel, primaries and digitalisation. Populism is now a field of its own, with the PopuList's binary classification for Europe, continuous expert scores (POPPA, V-Party) and speech-based measures of leaders (Global Populism Database).

Most of the 74 PARTY rows are recent, single-team datasets deposited on Harvard Dataverse, GESIS or Zenodo, and 38 are frozen after one release. Coverage is strongly European. Latin America has CHES-LA, PREPPS and the Mainwaring-Su volatility data, but Africa and Asia have little party-level data beyond V-Party and the Global Party Survey.

core.text: The Manifesto Project Dataset codes the share of each party manifesto devoted to 56 policy categories. It covers 67 countries from 1920 to 2025 in the 2026a release, and the same project distributes the annotated Manifesto Corpus and the manifestoR package. Its election-by-election coverage spans more than a century. Its known weaknesses are well documented. Emphasis is conflated with position, the additive left-right scale is biased toward the centre (Lowe, Benoit, Mikhaylov and Laver 2011), and single-coder classification error is substantial (Mikhaylov, Laver and Benoit 2012). Use scaled measures such as logit scales, or report uncertainty.

The Chapel Hill Expert Survey places European parties on general left-right, economic, cultural (GAL-TAN) and European integration dimensions, plus specific issues. Its trend file covers seven waves from 1999 to 2024, and separate surveys cover Latin America (2020) and candidate countries. It is widely used for European party positions on integration and on the cultural dimension. Expert placements may track reputations more than current policy (Budge 2000), and the wave design cannot capture change between surveys.

V-Party extends the V-Dem method to parties. Expert ratings of party identity, ideology, anti-pluralism, populism and organisation are aggregated with a measurement model that reports uncertainty. Coverage includes parties above about 5 percent of the vote in 178 countries from 1970 to 2019. This makes it a major source for party ideology and organisation outside Europe, but it has not been updated since its 2022 release.

Party Facts is a crosswalk, not a measurement dataset. It assigns a stable identifier to each core party and links it to the party codes of the Manifesto Project, ParlGov, CHES, V-Party, CLEA and dozens of other sources across 224 countries. Any study that combines party datasets should merge through it. Cite a dated Dataverse snapshot, because the web version changes continuously.

The PopuList classifies European parties since 1989 as populist, far right, far left or Eurosceptic, using expert judgment and literature review. Version 4.0 covers 31 countries to 2026. It is a common reference for party-family and populism counts in Europe. Its binary coding cannot capture degrees of populism, and the authors report only moderate agreement with POPPA for the far left.

choosing: Choose between manifesto and expert data according to the quantity of interest. Manifestos record what parties emphasise at each election; experts record where parties stand, as observers perceive it. The two correlate on general left-right but diverge on specific issues and on change over time. Results that hold under one family should be checked against the other.

Link every party dataset through Party Facts identifiers rather than party names. Note that expert surveys cover only parties above vote or seat thresholds, which excludes small and new parties from most position analyses.
gaps: Party-level data for Africa, the Middle East and much of Asia are scarce. V-Party and the Global Party Survey give single snapshots or long-interval coverage, and there is no African party-system dataset comparable to the European or Latin American ones.
Several global expert surveys (V-Party, Global Party Survey) have not been updated since 2019-2022, leaving recent party change outside Europe poorly measured.
Party organisation data rely on formal statutes or expert judgments; systematic data on party finances, membership and candidate selection in practice remain limited.
